text.p: Tobacco is a subject high on the agenda of many insurers this week as they await the outcome of talks between cigarette makers and U.S. attorneys general.

Expectations are mounting that a settlement could be reached this week which would give tobacco manufacturers immunity from class actions. In return the tobacco industry would make compensation payments for tobacco related illnesses and agree to a range of measures aimed at reducing the number of smokers.

Ever since the talks began in early April, there has been talk that insurers may be asked to contribute to compensation payments. The talk has been vague, but many insurers of tobacco companies have been quietly consulting their lawyers.
Insurers, including Lloyd's syndicates, say that much of their business with tobacco manufacturers was written on the basis that it excluded product liability claims.
Publicly, they are confident that they will not be asked to stump up money for any compensation deal, especially as no tobacco company has yet shown any sign of turning to its insurers.

Some observers doubt that the exclusion clauses would prove as watertight in U.S. courts as the industry hopes. Nonetheless, it would appear that insurers are in a stronger position than they were with issues such as U.S. environmental claims and asbestosis.

Although claims from these two events cost insurers dear, they did not sink the industry as some had predicted. Lloyd's of London suffered disproportionately from both risks, but is adamant that its potential exposure to tobacco is limited.
